title: Representatives Move to Force Action on Gift Ban
raw_text:
Representatives Move to Force Action on Gift Ban
September 28, 2026
HARRISBURG – Reps. Mike Jones (R-York), Marc Anderson (R-York) and Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon) today filed a discharge petition trying to force the House of Representatives to take votes on
House Bill 744
, a measure that would prohibit lawmakers, political candidates and government employees from accepting cash in any amount and gifts valued at more than $50.
The representatives consulted with MarchOnHarrisburg advocates as they developed the discharge petition to uphold the organization’s mission to get money out of politics in Pennsylvania.
“We know that money can influence, there are reasons lobbyists spend it, and it can have a very adverse effect on the public’s trust and perception of our legislative body here in Harrisburg. Those things matter. They matter a lot,” said Jones. “While allowing for common sense exceptions such as legitimate education opportunities related to legitimate legislative work, this bill eliminates cash gifts and puts forth very substantial restrictions on personal gifts, such as travel, sporting event tickets, and individual meals, none of which are necessary for any of us to perform our job as legislators,” he said.
Barger explained a large part of why he supports the petition is because of overall inaction in the Pennsylvania General Assembly.
“The House has been in voting session just 36 days this calendar year. We’re supposed to be a full-time Legislature, but House Democrats have given us few opportunities to be in Harrisburg and even fewer chances to consider worthy legislation like the gift ban and the multiple bills that would protect female athletes from competing against males,” Barger said. “We shouldn’t have to force it to happen. Why are we not here more often doing the work of the people?”
“Servant leadership is a critical element of self-government,” said Anderson. “One cannot effectively and honorably serve the people if they seek to serve themselves. The ban on legislative gifts is a step to return our focus on service to others instead of service to self.”
Jones said it’s quite rare for Republican lawmakers to force a vote on a Democrat bill. “While our actions cannot force the bill into law, it can force action on the bill; and it can force some, hopefully all members, to finally let us know where they stand on the gift ban. It’s time for an up- or- down vote. That’s all we want,” Jones said.
Jones filed the discharge petition at the Capitol this morning ahead of its formal introduction in the House.
They held a news conference to announce their intentions
.
Representative Mike Jones
93rd Legislative District
Representative Scott Barger
80th Legislative District
Representative Marc Anderson
92nd Legislative District

title: Focus on Data Centers: Barger, Verobish Tackle Tough Issues at Joint Event
raw_text:
Focus on Data Centers: Barger, Verobish Tackle Tough Issues at Joint Event
September 24, 2026
ALTOONA –
Reps. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon) and Andrea Verobish (R-Blair) today hosted an informational meeting about the anticipated proliferation of data centers across the United States, with a particular focus on how large-scale installations will impact the 13-state power grid that includes Pennsylvania.
Barger and Verobish addressed 200 constituents at the Blair County Convention Center, where they acknowledged concerns they’ve heard about environmental permitting, power and water usage, and the local controls established in statewide zoning laws.
Both representatives support the Ratepayer Protection Act – initiatives at both the state and federal level to ensure developers bring their own sources of new electric generation and meet other benchmarks.
“Sometimes it feels as if data center planning is outpacing sources of reliable information about the centers themselves. I’m thankful we could hold this meeting to share vetted, trustworthy information with our friends and neighbors,” Barger said.
“This next wave of development will require an all-hands-on-deck approach to ensure it is done responsibly,” Verobish said. “State lawmakers like us play a role, as do our partners in the federal government and local municipalities. Innovation and foresight are needed now more than ever.”

title: State Grant Funding Awarded Across Blair, Huntingdon Counties, Barger Says
raw_text:
State Grant Funding Awarded Across Blair, Huntingdon Counties, Barger Says
September 15, 2026
HARRISBURG — Local Share Account (LSA) grant funding has been awarded to five public safety, infrastructure and community development projects across the 80th District, according to Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon).
“Our local fire companies, police departments, municipal governments and healthcare providers are pillars of our region, and these grants strengthen the vital services they deliver every day,” Barger said. “Their work keeps our communities safe, connected and cared for. I’m pleased to announce projects that invest directly in the well being of residents of Blair and Huntingdon counties.”
“Securing funding for these projects strengthens public safety, improves emergency response, modernizes water and sewer systems, and ensures reliable municipal operations which will improve the quality of life for residents across the 30th district,” Senator Judy Ward said. “I’m pleased to have supported these grant applications, and grateful the CFA recognized their importance and awarded the funding.”
Approved projects include:
•	Blair County, $952,389 to purchase new mobile radios that will ensure reliable emergency communication for all 22 fire companies across the county.
•	Duncansville Borough, $65,844 to acquire a new police responder vehicle.
•	Huston Township, $600,000 to replace the deteriorated superstructure of Bridge No. 1 on Negley Spring Road.
•	Southern Alleghenies Planning & Development Commission, $175,000 to purchase and install a new digital X ray machine.
•	Warriors Mark Township, $150,000 to support construction of a new municipal building.
LSA grants are funded by state gaming revenue, not taxpayer dollars. The funding was approved by the Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA). This is an independent agency that holds fiduciary responsibility over the funding of programs and investments in Pennsylvania’s economic growth.
Questions about the grants can be directed to Barger’s office at 814-695-2398.

State Grant Funding Helps Preserve 80th District History, Barger Says
September 11, 2026
HARRISBURG
— State grant funding has been awarded to two organizations working to preserve the history of the 80th Legislative District, according to Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon).
The Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission (PHMC) awarded the grants through its Cultural and Historical Support Grant Program, which provides operating support to museums and historical organizations that preserve and share Pennsylvania’s heritage.
The Blair County Historical Society and the Huntingdon County Historic Society will each receive $9,500. The Blair County funding will help cover operational costs, including utilities and insurance, to support the Baker Mansion History Museum. In Huntingdon County, the grant will help pay for maintenance, conservation supplies and special exhibits.
“These grants support local historical preservation and enrich programming that serves residents and visitors alike,” Barger said. “Our county historical societies do a great job keeping history accessible, engaging and alive for future generations. I am glad to see their efforts supported by this funding.”

Verobish, Barger to Answer Questions about Data Centers
August 17, 2026
ALTOONA
– Reps. Andrea Verobish (R-Blair) and Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon) will host an informational meeting about data centers Thursday, Sept. 24, from 6:30-8 p.m. at the
Blair County Convention Center

The representatives intend to share a presentation about the state’s preparation for the projected influx of data centers, with a specific focus on the centers’ power needs. They will answer questions after the initial presentation.
“Every day, we read a new headline about data center development somewhere in Pennsylvania,” Barger said. “Lawmakers are considering several proposals that affect that development. In particular, there is bipartisan agreement these developers need to provide their own sources of electricity.”
“Regardless of where these centers are built, they have the potential to greatly impact our regional power grid. Our constituents are rightfully concerned about these centers being incorporated into Pennsylvania via smart, deliberate development,” Verobish said.
Barring technical difficulties, the informational meeting will be livestreamed at both RepBarger.com and RepVerobish.com.

title: Flood Victims Encouraged to Apply for State, Federal Assistance
raw_text:
Flood Victims Encouraged to Apply for State, Federal Assistance
July 23, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Residents and business owners impacted by the July 5-6 flash flooding may be eligible to take advantage of newly available state and federal disaster assistance, according to Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon).
The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) has approved the state’s request for disaster loans for individuals, businesses and nonprofit organizations affected by flooding in Blair, Bedford, Cambria, Centre, Clearfield and Huntingdon counties.
In addition, the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency has activated the Commonwealth Disaster Recovery Assistance Program (DRAP) for eligible homeowners and renters in the City of Altoona, Antis Township, Logan Township, Snyder Township, Tyrone Borough and Warriors Mark Township.
“Our communities have shown incredible resilience in the wake of these devastating floods,” Barger said. “I encourage everyone who suffered damage to explore these assistance programs and apply if they are eligible. These resources may help with the recovery process.”
The SBA has also opened a Disaster Loan Outreach Center at the Tyrone Borough offices, 1100 Logan Ave., to provide in-person application assistance through Aug. 13. Copies of paper applications can be requested through Barger’s office by calling 814-695-2398.
Applications for SBA physical damage loans are due Sept. 21. DRAP applications (intended for filers with lower income levels) will be accepted through Oct. 21.
Residents with unmet recovery needs may also contact PA 211 by dialing 2-1-1 for additional local assistance and support.

title: PA Budget Lacks Key Initiatives, Barger Says
raw_text:
PA Budget Lacks Key Initiatives, Barger Says
July 12, 2026
HARRISBURG –
The $50.8 billion 2026-27 budget passed by the House of Representatives today does not take appropriate steps to control spending, according to Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon).
“I had two priorities: saving the Rainy Day Fund and eliminating the structural deficit. It’s good we preserved the balance in the Rainy Day Fund, but we made no real effort to exercise fiscal restraint. I had to be a ‘no’ vote,” Barger said.
The budget as passed fails to address scholarships that could be used by families with students trapped in failing schools. It does not legalize and/or tax skill games that the state Supreme Court deemed illegal gaming devices without legislative regulation, meaning fraternal and veterans clubs benefiting from the games’ revenue will be harmed starting this fall.
Negotiations also did not advance a Senate bill that would have allowed local municipalities to place an 18-month moratorium on new data center development.
“I feel we should have done more and gone further to address important issues affecting the Commonwealth. The budget as written does not empower local stakeholders,” Barger said.
Barger expressed frustration that the budget, which passed both chambers this weekend, was yet again not finished by the June 30 deadline required of lawmakers.

title: Barger Amendment Addresses Non-Compete Agreements for Broadcasters
raw_text:
Barger Amendment Addresses Non-Compete Agreements for Broadcasters
June 30, 2026
HARRISBURG – In a move supported by the Pennsylvania Association of Broadcasters, Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon) attempted to amend
House Bill 2558
to lessen the detrimental impacts of potential ban on non-compete agreements on over-the-air television and radio news operations.
House Bill 2558, introduced by Rep. Ben Waxman (D-Philadelphia) would prohibit non-compete agreements in the contracts of broadcast workers seeking to change employment.
Barger tried to amend the legislation so that it would only affect workers who switch jobs within the same media market as defined by Nielsen. His proposal would cap the duration of non-compete agreements at six months.
“I sought to have a hearing on this legislation, so my fellow lawmakers could hear directly from the people this bill impacts. Frustratingly, that request was denied,” Barger said. “This bill without the amendment would be financially devastating to Pennsylvania’s broadcasters, particularly the smallest ones. They have enough stressors on their industry without this burden.”
The amendment was defeated on a party-line vote of 100-102.
House Bill 2558 (without the amendment) is scheduled for a House vote Wednesday, July 1.

title: Verobish, Barger Announce More Than $184,000 in Impact Fees to Support Blair County
raw_text:
Verobish, Barger Announce More Than $184,000 in Impact Fees to Support Blair County
June 17, 2026
BLAIR – More than $184,000, collected in natural gas impact fees in 2025, will be distributed among Blair County and its municipalities, Reps. Andrea Verobish (R-Blair) and Scott Barger (Blair/Huntingdon) announced today.
Blair County government will receive $144,491 and 25 municipalities will collectively receive $39,548.
“Having a rich natural gas industry in Pennsylvania plays a vital role in our economy and energy production. This funding continues that impact by investing directly in our communities,” Verobish said. “These fees are essential for supporting programs and projects in Blair County without placing any additional burden on taxpayers.”
Fees are collected from drilling companies with 60% returned to counties and municipalities affected by drilling. The other 40% goes into the Marcellus Shale Legacy Fund, which supports statewide environmental initiatives, greenways and infrastructure projects.
“Pennsylvania is fortunate to have so much natural gas right below our feet. Our state not only benefits from the natural gas industry’s contributions to our robust energy portfolio, but also these impact fees that help municipal governments provide services to our friends and neighbors,” Barger said.
Payments are expected to be distributed in early July.

title: Representatives Recommit to Preserving State’s Savings, Barger Says
raw_text:
Representatives Recommit to Preserving State’s Savings, Barger Says
June 3, 2026
HARRISBURG – Forty-three state representatives, including Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon), signed a pledge saying they will not vote for, support or advance any state budget that drains the Rainy Day Fund established in 2002 to address emergencies.
The signatories indicate they will oppose any use of the Rainy Day Fund to balance the budget, close structural deficits or fund recurring expenditures. They authored the pledge in response to Gov. Josh Shapiro’s proposal to increase state spending by $2.7 billion.
“Our constituents should be reassured that we recognize the true purpose of saving money in the Rainy Day Fund – to be used only for a rainy day,” Barger said. “The governor’s appetite to spend, spend, spend has already detrimentally affected the Rainy Day Fund. We need to protect it from further erosion.”
The Rainy Day Fund is projected to hold about $8 billion by the end of June. That represents about 53 days of state spending.
Signatories of the open letter to constituents note any use of the Rainy Day Fund requires a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly.
To read a copy of the letter, visit

title: Barger, Policy Committee Examine Childcare Affordability Crisis in Blair Co.
raw_text:
Barger, Policy Committee Examine Childcare Affordability Crisis in Blair Co.
May 1, 2026
HOLLIDAYSBURG
— The House Republican Policy Committee, led by Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata), convened a public hearing Thursday at the Blair Regional YMCA to examine the growing challenges surrounding childcare affordability and accessibility for Pennsylvania families. Hosted by Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon), the hearing featured testimony from childcare, business, education, and community leaders on staffing shortages, regulatory burdens, and rising costs impacting families and providers alike.
“As we travel the Commonwealth focused on affordability, we continue hearing that childcare is one of the biggest pressures facing Pennsylvania families,” said Rowe. “Parents are facing long waitlists and rising costs, while providers are struggling with staffing shortages, increasing expenses, and regulations that are often difficult to navigate. Our goal is to identify practical solutions that improve access to safe, high-quality childcare while supporting the providers families depend on.”
“The message we heard today was simple: families need childcare and providers want to serve them, but the system is making it harder than it needs to be,” Barger said. “Small regulatory barriers are creating big, real-world consequences for working parents.”
Testifiers at the hearing included:
•
Sharon Jones, executive director of the Blair Regional YMCA
•
Bill Young, director of compensation, benefits and risk for Sheetz
•
Mark Lingenfelter, lead pastor of Grace Fellowship Church
•
Rodney Green, founder of Rodney L. Green Consulting
Written testimony was submitted by Jolie L. Cover, president and executive director of Begin With Us Child Care and Preschool Inc. in Altoona.
Testifiers emphasized that childcare challenges extend beyond families and providers, impacting Pennsylvania’s workforce and economy as a whole.
Jones highlighted how outdated and inflexible regulations can limit childcare availability despite strong demand. Jones explained that minor regulatory adjustments could allow providers to serve additional children and reduce waitlists without compromising safety.
“We are committed to safety — that’s non-negotiable,” Jones testified. “But there are simple changes that could make a major difference for families, providers and employers throughout our communities.”
Young discussed the company’s employer-supported childcare model and the direct connection between reliable childcare and workforce stability.
“When childcare falls through, employees miss shifts, reduce hours or leave the workforce altogether,” Young testified. “This creates instability for families and real operational challenges for employers.”
Lingenfelter shared concerns about confusing and inconsistent state guidance impacting long-standing, faith-based preschool programs. Lingenfelter testified that his church’s preschool, which has served families in the community for more than 40 years, received conflicting information regarding changing compliance requirements.
“We do not seek to sidestep educational standards or safety requirements,” Lingenfelter said. “But the way state laws are implemented has just as much impact on families as the laws themselves.”
Educational consultant Rodney Green stressed that affordability has become a reality affecting families, employers and providers alike.
“Affordability is not a catchphrase,” Green testified. “It’s a reality for families, employees and employers.”
Testifiers also highlighted the role Pennsylvania’s Educational Improvement Tax Credit (EITC) program can play in expanding childcare access and supporting working families. Young noted that Sheetz utilizes EITC-supported scholarships to help offset childcare costs for employees using its on-site learning center, describing the program as an example of a successful public-private partnership that improves affordability while helping employers recruit and retain workers.
Throughout the hearing, lawmakers discussed the importance of maintaining safety and quality standards while identifying opportunities to modernize regulations, improve workforce pathways and reduce unnecessary barriers that limit childcare access.
“This is not about lowering standards,” Rowe said following the hearing. “It’s about finding the right balance, so families can access affordable childcare, providers can continue serving their communities and Pennsylvania’s workforce can thrive.”
With Thursday’s hearing, the Policy Committee has now convened five hearings focused on childcare affordability and accessibility.

title: Governor Demonstrates Delusion Related to State Spending, Barger Says
raw_text:
Governor Demonstrates Delusion Related to State Spending, Barger Says
February 3, 2026
HARRISBURG – When Gov. Josh Shapiro today proposed another $2.7 billion in state spending, Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair/Huntingdon) questioned whether the state’s top executive needs coursework in math.
“It might be helpful if the governor demonstrated a working understanding of basic economics and arithmetic before Pennsylvanians trust his evaluation that a 5.4% increase in spending is a good idea,” Barger said.
Despite an existing $4.8 billion structural deficit, Shapiro presented a $53.26 billion proposal to the Legislature. It would require raiding the state’s Rainy Day Fund (similar to a savings account) for another $4.58 billion.
“I wish this governor was as passionate about helping Pennsylvanians afford their exorbitant utility bills as he is about overspending us into a fiscal grave,” Barger said.
Barger firmly believes the state should not spend more than its projected revenues, which are estimated to increase by only 1.9%. He said he certainly does not believe Shapiro’s rosy projections for planned tax revenue from skills games, recreational marijuana and a higher minimum wage – particularly because these initiatives will meet strong resistance from the Legislature.
“Every time I heard the governor say the words ‘invest’ or ‘investment,’ I thought about how he wants to overspend,” Barger said.
Pennsylvania’s 2026-27 fiscal year starts July 1. For more information about the state budget or the upcoming Appropriations committee hearings, visit
